lessons.title: Why are you here? The compass of your values
lessons.summary: Your values show the direction of change.

slides.title: What does your compass show?
slides.text: Values are your compass for what matters in life: your relationship, your health, your focus, your faith, your work. Goals end one day; values always guide you.

slides.title: Direction, not rules
slides.text: Forcing yourself with rules often backfires. Values help you ask: “Does this behaviour bring me closer to what I care about?”

slides.title: Concrete sentences
slides.text: A concrete sentence like “Giving my evenings to sleep and my studies” instead of “focus” is a much stronger reminder in a hard moment.

slides.title: You don't have to be perfect
slides.text: Living by your values isn't being flawless every day; it's turning back towards them each time.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Think of the two values that matter most to you. For each one, write a small, concrete behaviour you could do this week.

quiz.q: How do values help in this process?
options: They wipe out the urge completely
They make me ask whether the behaviour brings me closer to what I care about
They're a yardstick for blaming myself
quiz.explain: Values don't erase the urge, but by reminding you which way you want to go, they make choosing easier.

slides.title: A chain
slides.text: Behaviour usually doesn't happen all at once. A trigger (place, time, feeling) comes first, then a thought, a feeling, an urge and finally the behaviour.

slides.title: Seeing the chain
slides.text: The better you know the chain, the easier it is to break it at an early link. Your phone in bed at night can be a trigger; “I'll just have a quick look” is a thought.

slides.title: Stepping in at an early link
slides.text: The easiest intervention is often at the very start: changing the trigger (taking the phone out of the room) or noticing the thought.

slides.title: Your chain
slides.text: Everyone's chain is a little different. Your diary helps you see the links in yours.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Think of the last time you struggled and write your chain: trigger → thought → feeling → urge → behaviour.

quiz.q: Where is it usually easiest to break the chain?
options: At the very end, in the middle of the behaviour
At the early links: the trigger or the thought
The chain can't be broken
quiz.explain: The earlier you notice, the easier it is to change.

lessons.title: Why does self-monitoring work?
lessons.summary: You can't change a pattern you can't see.

slides.title: Noticing is a skill
slides.text: Self-monitoring makes automatic behaviours visible. Research shows that keeping regular records supports change even on its own.

slides.title: What to record?
slides.text: The time, the place, the feeling before and what you felt afterwards. No need to write a lot; a few taps are enough.

slides.title: Data, not judgement
slides.text: A record isn't a report card. The aim isn't to criticise yourself but to see the pattern: “So I struggle at night when I'm tired.”

slides.title: The weekly view
slides.text: The weekly summary shows your riskiest hour and the tool that helps most. You adjust your plans accordingly.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Today, make at least one urge or behaviour entry; just to notice.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of keeping records?
options: To judge myself
To see patterns and adjust my plan to them
To collect points
quiz.explain: A record is a source of data; it shows when and why you struggle.

slides.title: Friction
slides.text: Making a behaviour even a little harder reduces how often it happens. Charging the phone in another room or moving a trigger app into a folder are brakes.

slides.title: Change what's easy
slides.text: Environment is stronger than willpower. So instead of resisting in a hard moment, it's smarter to make hard moments less likely to come.

slides.title: Filters are a brake
slides.text: Your phone's own filter and app timers help. No filter is unbeatable; the real strength is in your plan and your skills.

slides.title: Risky hours
slides.text: Preparing your environment in advance for your riskiest hours (light on, phone away, an activity planned) makes the biggest difference.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Choose one change you can make to your environment for your riskiest hour and do it this evening.

quiz.q: What is the logic of shaping your environment?
options: Resisting harder in a hard moment
Making hard moments less likely from the start
Filters solving everything
quiz.explain: Adding friction makes the moment of decision easier.

slides.title: Four states
slides.text: Urges come on stronger when we're Hungry, Angry (stressed or irritated), Lonely or Tired.

slides.title: Tiredness and night
slides.text: Lack of sleep reduces your ability to regulate yourself. That's why late at night is the riskiest time.

slides.title: Loneliness
slides.text: Loneliness is a common trigger. Even if the behaviour brings short relief, it often doesn't ease the loneliness.

slides.title: Look at the root
slides.text: When an urge comes, first ask yourself: which one is it? Sometimes a glass of water, a short nap or a phone call changes the urge.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Do a HALT check three times today and note what you notice each time.

quiz.q: When an urge comes while you're lonely, what helps to look at?
options: Suppressing the urge
The real need: making a connection
Nothing
quiz.explain: Meeting the need underneath the urge eases it more lastingly.

lessons.title: Urge surfing
lessons.summary: Being able to stay with the urge without fighting it.

slides.title: Like a wave
slides.text: Urges are like waves: they rise, peak and fall. They pass even when you don't act on them.

slides.title: Fighting is exhausting
slides.text: Trying to suppress an urge or not think about it often makes it bigger. ACT suggests watching the urge instead of fighting it.

slides.title: Watch it in your body
slides.text: Notice where in your body you feel the urge. Use your breath like a surfboard; stay on top of the wave.

slides.title: The choice is yours
slides.text: Feeling an urge doesn't mean you have to act on it. Feeling and choosing are separate things.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: When an urge comes, watch it like a wave and note how it changes. If you like, do it together with the breathing on the Urge moment screen.

quiz.q: What is the aim of urge surfing?
options: To get rid of the urge right away
To watch the urge and let it pass without acting on it
To try not to think about the urge
quiz.explain: Watching an urge is less tiring than fighting it and lets you choose your behaviour.

lessons.title: A thought is just a thought
lessons.summary: “Just once won't hurt”, “I've already ruined it”.

slides.title: The voice of the mind
slides.text: In hard moments the mind comes up with persuasive lines: “Just once won't hurt.” “I've already blown it, so it doesn't matter now.”

slides.title: Name it
slides.text: To put distance between you and the thought, name it: “Right now I'm noticing the thought ‘just once won't hurt’.”

slides.title: Like a radio
slides.text: You can think of thoughts like a radio playing in the background. You hear it, but you don't have to do everything it says.

slides.title: Come back to your values
slides.text: After noticing the thought, ask: “Does following this thought bring me closer to what I care about?”

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: This week, write down the sentence your mind comes up with most often and put “Right now I'm noticing the thought that …” in front of it.

quiz.q: What helps when the thought “I've already ruined it” comes?
options: Believing it and carrying on
Noticing it as a thought and coming back to your values
Blaming yourself
quiz.explain: Noticing the thought reminds you that you don't have to do what it says.

lessons.title: Acceptance: making room for uncomfortable feelings
lessons.summary: Carrying a feeling without trying to change it.

slides.title: Acceptance isn't giving up
slides.text: Acceptance isn't liking an uncomfortable feeling or giving in to it; it's being able to act in line with your values alongside it.

slides.title: Making room
slides.text: When tension, unease or a feeling of emptiness comes, notice it in your body and make a little room for it: “This feeling is here, and I can stay with it.”

slides.title: Feelings are temporary
slides.text: When we don't try to escape, feelings often change faster than we expect.

slides.title: The direction isn't lost
slides.text: Even with the uncomfortable feeling there, you can take a small values step: a walk, a message, a page of a book.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Watch an uncomfortable feeling for 60 seconds without trying to change it; then take a small values step.

options: Liking the uncomfortable feeling
Being able to stay with the uncomfortable feeling and act by my values
Giving up
quiz.explain: Acceptance is being able to make your choice without fighting the feeling.

lessons.title: Emotion regulation
lessons.summary: New ways for stress, anxiety and unease.

slides.title: A way of coping
slides.text: Behaviour is often a short escape from difficult feelings. That's very human; but in the long run it doesn't resolve the feeling.

slides.title: New tools
slides.text: Breathing or movement for stress, 5-4-3-2-1 awareness for anxiety, and writing to someone or a small task for unease can help.

slides.title: Name the feeling
slides.text: Even saying “I'm tense right now” lightens the brain's emotional load.

slides.title: Your own list
slides.text: Setting one or two new ways for each feeling means you know in advance what to do in a hard moment.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Write a new way of coping for each of the two feelings you struggle with most, and try one this week.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of naming a feeling?
options: It has no benefit
It lightens the feeling's load and opens up room to choose
It makes the feeling permanent
quiz.explain: Naming puts a little distance between you and the feeling.

lessons.title: The difference between shame and guilt
lessons.summary: Why shame doesn't work and self-compassion does.

slides.title: Two different feelings
slides.text: Guilt says “What I did didn't match my values.” Shame says “I'm bad.” They aren't the same.

slides.title: The shame cycle
slides.text: Shame makes a person feel bad, and feeling bad can trigger the search for escape again. Research shows that shame makes change harder.

slides.title: Self-compassion
slides.text: Self-compassion isn't excusing yourself; it's acknowledging your mistake and being as kind to yourself as you would be to a friend.

slides.title: Responsibility and kindness
slides.text: “This is a hard moment. I can make mistakes; I'm still carrying on.” This attitude makes it easier to take the next step.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Write a kind sentence you'll say to yourself in a hard moment and note it on your phone.

quiz.q: What is the difference between shame and guilt?
options: There's no difference
Guilt is about the behaviour, shame is about the person themselves
Shame is more useful
quiz.explain: Guilt focused on the behaviour opens room for change; shame aimed at the person often gets you stuck.

lessons.title: Sleep and a night routine
lessons.summary: Preparing for the riskiest time of day.

slides.title: Why at night?
slides.text: At night tiredness increases, things get quiet and the phone is in your hand. That's why late at night is the riskiest time.

slides.title: A calm routine
slides.text: Going to bed at a similar time every day, turning off screens before bed and dimming the light make sleep easier.

slides.title: Bed = sleep
slides.text: Not taking the phone to bed pairs the bed with sleep. If you can't sleep, getting up and reading a book in dim light can help.

slides.title: General information
slides.text: These are general sleep recommendations, not medical treatment. If your sleep problem lasts a long time, see a doctor.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Write a three-step night routine for this evening and follow it.

quiz.q: What is the easiest way to reduce night-time risk?
options: Going to bed with the phone and trying to resist
Leaving the phone outside the bedroom and setting up a calm routine
Going to bed later
quiz.explain: Shaping your environment in advance makes deciding easier at night.

slides.title: The need for connection
slides.text: People need connection. When loneliness grows, the search for short-term relief can grow too.

slides.title: Small steps
slides.text: Connection doesn't need big steps: a message, a short call, a coffee, a walk.

slides.title: Community
slides.text: A course, sport, volunteering or an interest group is a good way to have regular connection.

slides.title: Being open
slides.text: Even without giving details, you can tell someone you trust that you're struggling. A load you don't carry alone gets lighter.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: This week, message someone to meet face to face and set a day.

quiz.q: When you feel lonely, which helps more lastingly?
options: A short escape
Making a real connection
More screen time
quiz.explain: Connection meets the need underneath the urge.

slides.title: Gaps get filled
slides.text: When you cut down on a behaviour and the time it frees up stays empty, the old habit tries to come back into that gap.

slides.title: Movement
slides.text: Regular movement reduces stress and improves sleep. The fitness and breathing sessions in the app count too.

slides.title: Meaningful pursuits
slides.text: Learning something, making something or helping someone else gives satisfaction in line with your values.

slides.title: Planning
slides.text: Putting an activity in your risky hours in advance stops that time from being “empty”.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Plan an enjoyable or meaningful activity this week for one of your risky hours.

quiz.q: Why is it important to plan the free time that opens up?
options: It isn't important
Unplanned empty time makes it easier for the old habit to come back
To get more tired
quiz.explain: A planned activity fills the risky hour with new meaning.

lessons.title: A healthy view of sexuality
lessons.summary: Respect for yourself and your partner, realistic expectations.

slides.title: A natural part
slides.text: Sexuality is a natural part of human life. Masturbation itself isn't considered medically harmful; what matters is how the behaviour fits with your values and quality of life.

slides.title: Realistic expectations
slides.text: What's shown in pornography is often fiction and doesn't reflect real relationships. Knowing this makes expectations of yourself and your partner more realistic.

slides.title: Respect and communication
slides.text: The foundation of a healthy sex life is mutual consent, respect and open communication.

slides.title: For your concerns
slides.text: If you have a concern about sexual health, talking to a doctor or a professional is best, rather than claims on the internet.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Write a principle for yourself about “respect” and “realistic expectations”.

quiz.q: Which is true in this lesson?
options: The measure is what other people think
What matters is how the behaviour fits with my values and quality of life
Pornography reflects real relationships
quiz.explain: The measure is a person's own values and quality of life.

slides.title: Draw the map
slides.text: The relapse prevention model suggests recognising high-risk situations in advance: particular times, places, feelings and people.

slides.title: Early warnings
slides.text: A slip often starts with small signs: poor sleep, loneliness, the thought “I'll just have a look”.

slides.title: A plan for each situation
slides.text: Prepare an If–Then plan for each risky situation. A decision made in advance is much easier than one made in the moment.

slides.title: Slip ≠ the end
slides.text: If a slip happens, the thought “I've already blown it” can make it last longer. A slip doesn't mean your effort is erased; you can learn from it and carry on.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Write down your three riskiest situations and make an If–Then plan for each.

quiz.q: What attitude helps most after a slip?
options: Saying “I've already blown it, so it doesn't matter”
Learning what happened, updating the plan and carrying on
Giving up on everything
quiz.explain: Seeing a slip as a chance to learn makes it easier to carry on.

lessons.title: Your new identity
lessons.summary: “I'm someone who lives by my values.”

slides.title: From behaviour to identity
slides.text: Small, repeated behaviours change how we see ourselves over time.

slides.title: Who do you want to be?
slides.text: Being “someone who lives by my values” instead of “someone trying not to do this” shifts the focus from prohibition to direction.

slides.title: The evidence
slides.text: Every urge moment you've managed, every boundary you've set and every plan you've followed in this process is evidence of this new identity.

slides.title: Keeping it up
slides.text: Identity isn't something earned once and done; it's confirmed again every day through small choices.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Complete the sentence “I'm someone who …” in line with your values and write three pieces of evidence from this process.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of identity-focused thinking?
options: It shifts the focus from prohibitions to values and direction
It has no benefit
It makes being perfect a requirement
quiz.explain: Defining yourself by your values makes the behaviour more natural.

lessons.title: Being at peace with your values

slides.title: A feeling of conflict
slides.text: When a behaviour conflicts with your values, you may feel inner tension. This feeling shows what matters to you.

slides.title: The perfection trap
slides.text: Research shows that intense moral conflict and shame can lead people to see themselves as more “out of control”; this perception doesn't always match the amount of the behaviour.

slides.title: Direction is enough
slides.text: The aim isn't to become perfect overnight; it's to live a little closer to your values every day.

slides.title: Be kind to yourself
slides.text: Whatever your values, faith or principles, being kind to yourself is your strongest helper on this path.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Write a small step you could take today for one of your values; it doesn't have to be perfect.

options: Becoming perfect immediately
Not perfection, but a direction towards your values
Criticising yourself harshly
quiz.explain: Direction and self-compassion make change sustainable.
